overview: Rolls-Royce Holdings designs, manufactures and services gas turbine engines and power systems through three divisions: Civil Aerospace (large widebody and business aviation engines), Defence (military aero engines, naval propulsion, UK nuclear submarine reactors) and Power Systems (mtu-branded diesel/gas gensets and battery storage for data centres, governmental, marine and industrial markets). The Group also holds a stake in Rolls-Royce SMR, developing small modular nuclear reactors in the UK and Czech Republic. Revenue is global (UK, US, Germany engineering hubs; customers in over 100 countries), reported in GBP, with FY2025 underlying revenue of £20.1bn.

business_model.summary: Classic 'razor and blade' aerospace/defence model: engines are often sold near or below cost (original equipment, OE) while the large majority of profit comes from decades-long aftermarket services (spare parts, overhauls, long-term service agreements/LTSAs tied to flying hours). Power Systems sells gensets (OE) plus services, with a fast-growing data-centre back-up power niche. Defence revenue splits between OE and sustainment, heavily government-funded with multi-decade programme visibility (UK nuclear submarines, EJ200, AE engine family).
business_model.customer_type: B2B/B2G: airlines and lessors, aircraft OEMs (Airbus, Boeing, Gulfstream, Bombardier), governments/defence ministries (UK MoD, US DoW, NATO allies), data centre operators and industrial/marine customers
business_model.geographic_mix: Engineering and manufacturing concentrated in the UK, US and Germany; sales and services global with roughly a third from the Americas, significant exposure to Europe and Asia-Pacific airlines and defence customers
business_model.revenue_characteristics: Highly recurring aftermarket/services revenue (LTSAs, time-and-materials shop visits) layered on cyclical, lower-margin OE sales; Defence has multi-year government contract backlog; Power Systems order coverage for 2026 already at 79%

main_competitors: GE Aerospace (incl. CFM joint venture with Safran)
competitive_position.market_position: Effective duopoly with GE Aerospace in large widebody engines -- every new-generation widebody is powered exclusively by Rolls-Royce or GE/CFM; Rolls-Royce has captured over 50% of widebody OE deliveries over the last three years, lifting installed fleet share from 34% to 38%. Sole supplier of nuclear propulsion for all UK Royal Navy submarines. Leading SMR developer in Europe (only company with contracted SMR programmes in both UK and Czech Republic). 20-25% share in data-centre/mission-critical back-up power and 30% in land/naval governmental diesel propulsion via Power Systems (mtu).

moat_factors.factor: High switching costs / long-lived installed base
moat_factors.description: Engines remain in service for decades; airlines and militaries are locked into OEM-specific MRO ecosystems, spare parts and LTSAs once an engine is selected
Aero engine certification is extremely costly and slow, and sovereign nuclear propulsion for UK submarines is a government-mandated single-source relationship
Decades of accumulated IP in turbine design, materials and nuclear propulsion; UltraFan and SMR programmes extend the technology lead
Sole engine supplier on platforms like the A350 (Trent XWB); duopoly structure limits competitive bidding on many widebody programmes
Deep, multi-decade partnerships with UK/US/allied defence ministries and the UK's Great British Energy-Nuclear programme for SMRs

weaknesses: Concentration risk in a few aircraft platforms and a handful of large airline/defence customers
OE engine sales are frequently loss-making or low-margin, making the model dependent on aftermarket execution and time-on-wing improvements
History of costly technical/durability issues (e.g., Trent 1000 Package C) that damaged the brand and consumed years of remediation capital
Smaller scale than GE Aerospace in overall revenue and R&D budget
SMR and new-technology bets (UltraFan, narrowbody re-entry, Series 4000) require years of capital before any payback and carry execution risk

growth_drivers: Widebody aftermarket: rising Trent XWB/Trent 1000/Trent 700 flying hours, LTSA margin expansion (contract margin +19pts, in-year LTSA margin +28pts vs 2022 baseline) and time-on-wing initiatives targeting >100% improvement
Business aviation momentum: Pearl-powered Gulfstream G700/G800, Bombardier Global 5500/6500, and continued Pearl 10X certification progress

Defence order ramp: EJ200 export wins (Turkiye, Italy, Germany, Spain), AUKUS submarine programme, GCAP (next-generation fighter) co-development, MV-75/FLRAA and B-52 re-engining (F130) in the US, growing autonomous-platform opportunities (MQ-25A, Orpheus)

Power Systems data-centre supercycle: power generation OE revenue growth targeted at ~20% p.a., driven by AI/hyperscaler back-up and prime power demand; new Series 4000 engine launching 2028 with 20% higher power density

Rolls-Royce SMR: contracted programmes in the UK (Great British Energy-Nuclear, Wylfa, three units, GBP2.6bn government allocation) and Czech Republic (CEZ, Temelin), strategic investment from CEZ Group, addressable market of 400+ SMRs by 2050, plus adjacent Advanced Modular Reactor opportunity
Narrowbody re-entry option via UltraFan technology demonstrator (ground testing planned 2028)

Capital returns: multi-year GBP7.0-9.0bn share buyback programme 2026-2028 plus reinstated/growing dividend, supported by net cash position and investment-grade ratings (upgraded by Moody's to A3 and Fitch to A- in 2026)

business.description: A relatively small number of aircraft programmes (A350, A330neo, 787 competing engine, business jets) and large airline/OEM customers drive a disproportionate share of profit
History of costly in-service problems (e.g., Trent 1000) shows execution risk in bringing new designs to full reliability; continued remediation investment required

business.risk: Competitive intensity from GE Aerospace/CFM and Pratt & Whitney
business.description: Engine selection on new aircraft platforms is infrequent and winner-take-most; losing a future sole-source position would be a multi-decade setback
Ongoing portfolio simplification (sale to Fairbanks Morse Defense) carries execution and continuity risk, though largely complete

financial.description: Large legacy defined-benefit pension obligations remain on the balance sheet despite de-risking progress
Significant USD revenue/cost mismatch; underlying results depend on hedging via forward contracts that lock in rates, creating timing/mark-to-market volatility
GBP7-9bn multi-year buyback and growing dividend reduce balance-sheet flexibility if end markets deteriorate

regulatory.description: Rolls-Royce SMR programmes in the UK, Czech Republic and prospective US market depend on multi-year regulatory licensing processes that could slip

regulatory.risk: Export controls and defence procurement policy
regulatory.description: Defence revenue is exposed to government budget cycles, procurement rules and export licensing (e.g., GCAP, EJ200 exports) in the UK, US, Japan, Italy and allied nations
Net zero commitments and sustainable aviation fuel mandates require continued product and operational investment

macro.description: US tariff announcements in 2025-2026 created cost and supply-chain uncertainty; company says it is mitigating but not immune
Aerospace-wide supply chain constraints (forgings, castings, titanium, semiconductors) persist; geopolitical tension (Russia, Taiwan) adds risk to critical material sourcing

Widebody OE deliveries and flying hours (which drive aftermarket revenue) are sensitive to global GDP, fuel prices, and geopolitical/conflict disruption (management cited Middle East conflict as a 2026 headwind partially offset by resilience)
Net cash position and investment-grade ratings reduce direct rate sensitivity, though pension discount rates and financing costs for customers/lessors matter indirectly

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Commercial aerospace aftermarket in multi-year upcycle as widebody fleets expand and flying hours recover/grow; global defence spending rising (NATO commitments, UK Defence Investment Plan); data-centre/AI-driven power demand creating a structural growth market for back-up and prime power generation; nuclear SMRs emerging as a new long-duration growth vector
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - Civil Aerospace OE is cyclical with airline capex and travel demand, but aftermarket/LTSA revenue is more resilient and tied to flying hours; Defence and nuclear submarine work is largely non-cyclical, government-funded; Power Systems data-centre demand currently structurally growing
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct (net cash balance sheet, investment-grade ratings), moderate indirect via customer financing costs and pension discount rate assumptions

recent_developments.event: H1 2026 results: underlying revenue up 26% organically to GBP11.3bn, operating profit up 46% to GBP2.5bn (22.5% margin, +3.1pts), free cash flow up 24% to GBP2.0bn, net cash GBP2.1bn; FY2026 guidance raised to GBP4.7-4.9bn underlying operating profit and GBP3.8-4.0bn free cash flow (from GBP4.0-4.2bn/GBP3.6-3.8bn at FY2025 results); interim dividend raised to 6.0p from 4.5p
Moody's upgraded credit rating to A3 and Fitch to A-, reflecting strengthened balance sheet; S&P also investment grade
Rolls-Royce and Reliance Industries announced intent to partner on an indigenous combat engine for India's AMCA fighter programme, including a dedicated Aero Gas Turbine Complex in India
Completed roughly $1bn multi-year investment in Indianapolis, US, expanding engine manufacturing/test capability supporting B-52 re-engining (F130) and MV-75/FLRAA (AE 1107F) programmes
Philippine Airlines order for 18 Trent XWB-97 engines; Somon Air MoU for Trent 1000 XE

Rolls-Royce SMR signed a two-stage UK contract with Great British Energy-Nuclear for three SMR units at Wylfa, Anglesey (GBP2.6bn government allocation) and an Early Works Contract with CEZ for the first Czech SMR programme at Temelin
Completed GBP200m interim share buyback (started January 2026), part of the GBP2.5bn tranche planned for 2026 within the GBP7.0-9.0bn 2026-2028 multi-year buyback programme
Completed the GBP1bn share buyback announced alongside FY2024 results

FY2025 results: underlying revenue GBP20.1bn (+12%), operating profit GBP3.46bn (17.3% margin, three years ahead of the original 15-17% mid-term target), free cash flow GBP3.27bn, net cash GBP1.9bn, order backlog GBP88.1bn; FY2025 full-year dividend of 9.5p; mid-term (2028) targets upgraded to GBP4.9-5.2bn operating profit, 18-20% margin, GBP5.0-5.3bn free cash flow, 23-26% return on capital
Completed sale of naval propulsors business to Fairbanks Morse Defense (naval handling business sale expected to complete in 2026)

items.notes: Raised from GBP4.0-4.2bn guidance given at FY2025 results (Dec 2025/Feb 2026), reflecting a strong H1 2026 (operating profit +46% yoy to GBP2.5bn)
Upgraded from original GBP2.5-2.8bn (set Nov 2023) via an interim 15-17% margin target that was itself exceeded three years early in 2025
Raised from 15-17% target set one year prior; FY2025 actual margin of 17.3% already exceeded the old range
Upgraded mid-term target disclosed with FY2025 results
Announced with FY2025 results; GBP1.4bn of the 2026 GBP2.5bn tranche completed by H1 2026 results

items.metric: Power Systems power generation OE growth
items.notes: Driven by data centre back-up/prime power demand
Raised from previous 12-14% guidance given rising global defence spending

items.target: Continuing improvement via aftermarket/LTSA margin expansion
items.notes: Qualitative guidance; widebody installed fleet share targeted to keep rising from 38%
FY2025 actual 14.4%; growth driven by self-help, productivity and capacity expansion

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Tufan Erginbilgic framed 2025 as a third successive year of record performance, explicitly describing the business as undergoing 'transformation' rather than a 'turnaround.' Management raised FY2026 and mid-term (2028) guidance twice within roughly seven months (Dec 2025 and again Jul 2026), citing strong operational execution, LTSA margin gains, time-on-wing improvements, and data-centre-driven Power Systems growth, while acknowledging an uncertain external environment (tariffs, supply chain constraints, and in H1 2026 commentary, the Middle East conflict) as manageable headwinds rather than reasons to lower guidance.

bull_case: Durable duopoly position with GE Aerospace in widebody engines, with rising installed base share (34% to 38% over three years) feeding a decades-long high-margin aftermarket annuity

Guidance has been raised twice in under a year and management has consistently beaten its own targets (mid-term margin target hit three years early in 2025), suggesting conservative goal-setting and genuine operational turnaround momentum

Multiple distinct growth vectors beyond the core civil aerospace cycle: Defence order backlog and NATO/AUKUS-driven spending, Power Systems data-centre/AI power demand (~20% p.a. targeted growth), and an emerging SMR nuclear business with contracted UK/Czech programmes and a 400+ unit addressable market by 2050
Strong balance sheet (net cash, investment-grade ratings upgraded by Moody's and Fitch in 2026) funding a large GBP7-9bn multi-year buyback alongside a growing dividend
High barriers to entry (certification costs, sovereign nuclear relationships, decades-long platform lock-in) protect the moat from new entrants
bear_case: Valuation has re-rated sharply on the transformation narrative; further upside requires continued flawless execution against already-raised guidance, leaving limited room for disappointment
History of costly in-service technical problems (e.g., Trent 1000) shows that new engine programmes (Trent XWB-97, UltraFan, Series 4000, SMR) carry real execution and reputational risk

Heavy reliance on a small number of aircraft platforms and government programmes; losing a future sole-source position or facing a defence budget pullback would be a multi-year setback given programme lead times
SMR and narrowbody re-entry bets require years of capital investment before any proven payback, and are dependent on third-party regulatory approval timelines outside the company's control
Macro/geopolitical risks (tariffs, titanium/supply chain disruption, conflict-driven demand volatility) could pressure margins even as management currently describes them as manageable
